title: Email Collection: Email Forwarding Rule
summary: Email forwarding rule abuse is the creation of a mailbox level rule so that incoming mail is copied or redirected to an address the adversary controls. The rule is stored in the mailbox on the server, not on the endpoint, so it keeps working after a password reset, after session tokens are revoked, and after the user's laptop is rebuilt. Rules can be created from the desktop mail client, from the web interface, by command line tooling, or by an administrator acting on many mailboxes at once. The Microsoft Messaging API (MAPI) can also be used to set rule properties so that the rule is marked hidden and never appears in the client. Defenders see rule creation in mailbox audit records and organisation wide transport rule changes in administrative logs, and separate malicious rules from ordinary ones by the destination domain, the scope of the rule, and a rule that exists in the server configuration but not in the client interface.

beginner.definition: An email forwarding rule is a setting inside a mailbox. It tells the mail server what to do with messages as they arrive. It can copy or move a message to another address automatically. An attacker who gets into a mailbox can add one. Copies of the victim's mail then keep arriving, even after the password has been changed.
beginner.whyItMatters: A forwarding rule turns one stolen password into a long term stream of the victim's email. It keeps working after a password reset, because the rule lives in the mailbox. It is not tied to the attacker's session. It is quiet, so nobody notices until someone reads the mailbox settings. Important mail such as invoices, password resets and contracts can flow out for months.
howItWorks: The attacker signs in to the mailbox with stolen credentials, using the mail client, the web page, or a script.
Inside the mailbox settings, the attacker creates a rule. It matches incoming messages, such as all mail or mail about payments.
The rule action forwards a copy to an address outside the company, or to another mailbox inside it.
The mail server applies the rule to every new message, so the copy leaves before the user reads anything.
A careful attacker uses the Messaging API. This interface lets programs manage mail, and it can mark the rule hidden from the client.
An administrator can also create rules for many mailboxes at once. These are called transport rules, and they run on all incoming mail.
beginner.example: Think of a shared flat with one post box for everyone. You can leave a note for the postman. It says: while I am away, send a copy of my letters to this other address. The postman keeps doing it even after you change the front door lock. The note is about the post box, not about the key. Nobody in the flat sees the letters going out. Only the post office's own records show that a redirection was set up, and only if someone thinks to look.
takeaways: Forwarding rules live in the mailbox, so resetting a password does not remove them.
Check the destination of every rule, especially addresses outside your organisation.
A rule can be hidden from the mail client, so compare the server settings with what the user sees.

objectives: Explain how a mailbox forwarding rule lets an attacker keep receiving a victim's email.
Describe which mailbox audit records and administrative logs show that a rule was created.
Distinguish a malicious forwarding rule from a legitimate user rule such as an out of office reply.
Explain why a password reset alone does not remove a forwarding rule.
Describe how a rule can be hidden through the Messaging API and why that matters for detection.
